questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] a durable workflow engine that survives crashes and deploys (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/18). Customers build onboarding workflows in a visual builder and add or reorder steps whenever they like; a webhook starts a run; steps send an email, post to a chat channel and book a calendar slot through three vendors, and some runs wait days for a human approval. Node rotations SIGKILL pods mid-step and the queue redelivers stalled jobs; one heavy workflow emits 50k progress events per run. Write your design before you look: what is the source of truth and what the queue carries, how a resumed run knows what already happened, how each vendor call stays safe to repeat, how two workers on one run are kept apart, where waits live, how failure ends, and what keeps the run history fast. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The run row in Postgres is the truth: the webhook writes it first and the queue message carries only a pointer to it, so a redelivered or lost message never holds state that exists nowhere else.
keyPoints.quote: Postgres is the source of truth

keyPoints.text: [w3] Each run pins the definition version it started on; resuming an in-flight run on the newest definition skips one side effect and repeats another once a step is inserted at the front, because positional step ids shift.
keyPoints.quote: In-flight runs resume on the version they started with

keyPoints.text: [w3] The completed-step lookup happens on every delivery before any step executes, whether or not the queue thinks this is a retry.
keyPoints.quote: Read the checkpoint before every side effect.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A checkpoint only shrinks the danger to the one step in flight; closing it needs a dedupe key derived from run and step that is sent to the vendor along with the call itself.
keyPoints.quote: A checkpoint narrows the window to one in-flight step

keyPoints.text: [w2] A worker renews its lease by heartbeat and stamps its writes with a fencing token, so a paused worker that wakes up late cannot overwrite the new owner's progress.
keyPoints.quote: its writes carry a fencing token so a zombie worker's late writes are rejected

keyPoints.text: [w2] Multi-day waits are rows in the database with a due time and a sweeper that wakes them, not an in-process timer or a queue delay that dies with the pod.
keyPoints.quote: Durable timers live in the DB

keyPoints.text: [w2] Retries are bounded and end in a terminal parked state with an alert, otherwise a failing run loops and grows history without limit (for illustration, relay's lab incident added about 3M history rows).
keyPoints.quote: must not loop forever; add DLQ/parking and an alert

keyPoints.text: [w1] Run history is a performance budget: heartbeat events and large outputs are offloaded, compacted and paged, or the run page degrades (for illustration, relay's lab measured a 3.4 s run page at 50k events).
keyPoints.quote: History growth is a performance problem.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — a node rotation SIGKILLs pods in the middle of steps, a teammate 'optimises' the resume path, a vendor answers with Retry-After while the worker is about to be rotated, and two processes end up resuming the same run. What breaks first, how does it show, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Killed after the vendor accepted the call but before the step's checkpoint committed: redelivery re-executes that step, and a vendor that receives no key (relay's chat connector) posts a second time.

[w3] Gating the checkpoint lookup on the queue's attempt counter skips it after a stall, because a stalled redelivery does not bump that counter; whether a run is resuming has to be derived from Postgres state.
keyPoints.quote: that counter is 0 on every delivery

keyPoints.text: [w2] A Retry-After wait held as an in-process sleep is lost when the worker dies; only stall redelivery restarts the run from its checkpoint.
keyPoints.quote: the wait is lost; only stall redelivery restarts the run from its checkpoint

keyPoints.text: [w2] The damage does not show in run status: a run that re-executed completed steps still ends succeeded, so the signal is in the event history (a second run start followed by steps that had already completed) and in per-vendor side-effect counts, and monitoring that watches status alone misses it.
keyPoints.quote: Read the events, not the status.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Without fencing, two resumers of one run both write its history, and if event writes are fire-and-forget with their errors swallowed, the conflicting writes silently lose events, so the history used for diagnosis cannot be trusted.
keyPoints.quote: The event log can drop events silently.

keyPoints.text: [w1] The retry budget must exist end to end, not just in a comment: if the queued message itself carries no retry attempts, a run that throws stays failed, whatever the code says about a retried delivery resuming it.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your engine against the alternatives the chapter names: checkpoint-and-skip vs event-history replay, leases with fencing vs relying on the queue's own lock, a vendor's declared dedupe window vs a key you send, and keeping large outputs in the run table vs offloading them. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Checkpoint-and-skip is the simpler resume model, but it only works if step identity is stable: ids based on position collide as soon as someone edits the definition.
keyPoints.quote: positional step ids collide when a definition changes

keyPoints.text: [w3] Event-history replay re-runs the workflow code against what was recorded, and the price is determinism: no clock reads, randomness or I/O outside activities.
keyPoints.quote: re-run workflow code against the recorded history

keyPoints.text: [w3] Relying on the queue's own lock costs nothing to build but does not stop a worker that lost it from writing; a lease plus fencing token makes the database reject the stale writer, and the price is a heartbeat every worker must keep renewing (more writes, and history bloat if heartbeats are recorded as events), a token checked on every state write, and a lease length to tune between fencing out slow-but-alive workers and leaving a dead worker's run idle.
keyPoints.quote: A worker holds a lease it renews by heartbeat

keyPoints.text: [w2] A dedupe window the vendor declares but nothing enforces is not idempotency: either enforce it yourself or label the step honestly as able to repeat.

[w2] Offloading large outputs keeps the run table small, but it turns the checkpoint into a pointer: if the store behind it is less durable than the checkpoint, a resume in another process finds the pointer and gets nothing back. Inline outputs cost table size and page speed; offloading costs a second store that must be as durable as Postgres.
keyPoints.quote: A durable checkpoint points at non-durable storage.
